analysis.one_liner: Bars governments from restricting abortion care before fetal viability and protects travel across state lines for abortion services.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 217 House Democrats and no Republicans, never received a committee or floor vote and died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have stopped federal, state, and local governments from banning abortion before fetal viability and from imposing rules that single out abortion care — things like mandatory waiting visits, requirements for medically unnecessary tests, and limits on medication abortion or telehealth. After viability, states could ban abortion except when a provider judges it necessary to protect the patient's life or health. It would have overridden inconsistent state laws, recognized a right to travel between states for care, and let the Justice Department, patients, and providers sue states to enforce it.
analysis.who_benefits: People who can become pregnant — especially the millions living in states where abortion is banned or heavily restricted — would regain access to care without traveling out of state or navigating state-imposed obstacles. Health care providers, including clinics, telehealth services, and pharmacies, would be able to provide abortion care without facing state bans, penalties, or lawsuits.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People needing abortions, especially in ban states

how_it_helps.text: Governments could not prohibit abortion before fetal viability, restrict specific abortion procedures or drugs, or block telemedicine abortion, and could not require medically unnecessary in-person visits, tests, or medically inaccurate counseling [S2].
After viability, states could restrict abortion only outside cases where a provider judges it necessary to protect the patient's life or health [S2].
The bill recognizes a right to travel to another state, including to obtain abortion services, and a right to help someone else obtain care [S2][S3].

It supersedes inconsistent federal and state laws, and the Justice Department, individuals, or providers can sue states or officials to enforce it, with states stripped of immunity and prevailing plaintiffs awarded attorney's fees [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: State governments — particularly the 14 states identified in the bill's findings as having no abortion provider — would lose the power to ban or restrict abortion care, and laws their legislatures passed would be invalidated. People who oppose abortion on moral or religious grounds would see state bans and restrictions struck down nationwide.

drawbacks.text: The bill would wipe out nearly all state abortion restrictions before viability in one stroke, overriding laws enacted by state legislatures and voters, which critics say removes citizens' ability to set abortion policy in their own states [S2][S3].

After viability, the only limit the bill guarantees is when the treating provider judges abortion necessary for the patient's life or health, and courts must weigh whether restrictions impede access using factors like travel and cost burdens — a standard critics argue makes virtually all regulation unenforceable [S2][S3].

The bill rests on contested legal ground: it invokes Congress's commerce and Fourteenth Amendment powers to preempt state law and strips states of immunity from suit, which opponents say exceeds constitutional limits and would face immediate court challenges [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For supporters, the gains are large and concrete: the bill's own findings describe 14 states where abortion was unavailable and 17.8 million women of reproductive age without access, plus sharply longer travel times and higher costs of time off work, child care, and lodging [S3]. The costs fall mainly on state sovereignty — states would lose their chosen abortion policies — and on people who believe abortion should be restricted. The bill offers no compromise mechanism for states to opt in or out; it is a full federal preemption of pre-viability abortion policy. Whether that trade is worth it depends entirely on where one stands on abortion itself.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to two House committees in March 2023 and to a Health subcommittee a week later, and the Republican-controlled House never took it up, so it expired when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 30, 2023, by Rep. Judy Chu and referred to the House Energy and Commerce and Judiciary Committees [S1][S5].
On April 7, 2023, it was referred to the Health Subcommittee, and no further action appears in the record — no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote [S5].
All 216 cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican signed on [S4].
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and the bill died with it [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: State officials and lawmakers in states with abortion bans and restrictions, whose laws remained in force because the bill never advanced; opponents of abortion access were better off, while people in ban states gained nothing.

for.name: Rep. Judy Chu
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited an initial bloc of more than 200 Democratic cosponsors on day one.

for.name: 216 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Every cosponsor of the bill was a House Democrat, giving it the support of roughly half the chamber's majority party but no Republicans.

for.name: Abortion rights groups
for.role: National advocacy organizations supporting abortion access
for.what_they_did: Publicly campaigned for federal legislation to restore nationwide abortion access after the Dobbs decision.

against.name: House Republican majority
against.role: Majority party controlling House committees and the floor calendar, 118th Congress
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a committee markup or floor vote on the bill; it sat in subcommittee from April 2023 until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The split was entirely by party: all 216 cosponsors plus the sponsor were Democrats, no Republican supported it, and the Republican-controlled House gave it no action after the initial referral [S4][S5].

industries.industry: Abortion providers (clinics, telehealth services, and pharmacies dispensing medication abortion)
industries.note: The bill would let providers offer abortion care in states that currently ban it, shield them from state penalties, and give them standing to sue states with attorney's fees awarded to prevailing plaintiffs [S2][S3]. The providers' interest in being able to practice runs alongside patients' interest in getting care.
States with abortion bans or restrictions would lose that authority entirely before viability, and their officials could be sued personally for enforcing those laws [S2][S3].
